name: Amiwo
subtitle: Amiwo, known in French as Beninese red paste, is a corn-flour dish cooked in a tomato sauce and is one of the main dishes of Benin households.

facts.label: Place in daily life
facts.value: Amiwo has been, from its origins to today, one of the main dishes of Benin households

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: A ritual dish from the Vodoun convents

facts.label: Change over time
facts.value: Red palm oil was once its main ingredient; it was replaced by tomato sauce

facts.label: Link to Ouidah
facts.value: Identical to the Afro-Brazilian (Agouda) cuisine of Ouidah

facts.label: How it is made
facts.value: Corn flour is stirred into a boiling tomato sauce, worked quickly with a wooden spatula, then set in oiled moulds and turned out onto a plate with a sautéed sauce

facts.label: Name
facts.value: Known in French as the Beninese red paste (pâte rouge)

facts.label: Ceremonies
facts.value: Under the name Bomiwô, the source describes a corn-flour dish long reserved by Vodun convents for ceremonies and often served with chicken

parts.text: Amiwo, known in French as Beninese red paste, is a corn-flour dish cooked in a tomato sauce and is one of the main dishes of Benin households. It began as a ritual dish of the Vodoun convents, made then with red palm oil, which tomato sauce later replaced, and it matches the Afro-Brazilian (Agouda) cooking of Ouidah.
It is set in oiled moulds, turned out onto a plate with a sautéed sauce, and is often served with chicken.
